findings.proposition: In its statement of intended proof (Exhibit A.2 to the proposed pretrial order), Qorvo states it is owed patent damages of $279,808 for Akoustis' infringement of the '755 and '018 Patents for 5 October 2021 through 30 June 2024, plus supplemental damages and post-verdict infringement at a 1% rate on Akoustis's accused product revenues, and that Akoustis's infringement was willful, entitling Qorvo to treble damages.
findings.target: Qorvo v. Akoustis, D. Del. 1:21-cv-01417: Qorvo's requested patent-infringement damages
findings.speaker: Qorvo

spans.quote: Qorvo is owed damages of $279,808 for Akoustis’ infringement of the ’755 and ’018 Patents for the period of October 5, 2021 through June 30, 2024.

Since obtaining knowledge of the ’018 Patent, Akoustis’s infringement has been willful, deliberate, and intentional, and Akoustis is acting in reckless disregard of Qorvo’s patent rights, entitling Qorvo to treble damages.
through the Court’s decision regarding the imposition of a permanent injunction and for post- verdict infringement at a rate of 1% applies to Akoustis’s accused product revenues.

findings.proposition: In its statement of intended proof, Qorvo states that the asserted trade secrets gave Akoustis a 55-month head start, that Akoustis has been unjustly enriched by at least $66.1 million as a result, and that the misappropriation was willful and malicious, entitling Qorvo to enhanced damages under the DTSA and NCTSPA.
findings.target: Qorvo v. Akoustis, D. Del. 1:21-cv-01417: Qorvo's requested trade-secret unjust-enrichment and exemplary damages
findings.speaker: Qorvo

spans.quote: Akoustis has been unjustly enriched by at least $66.1 million as a result of its 55- month head start.
As a result, Qorvo is entitled to enhanced damages under both the DTSA and the NCTSPA.
the Asserted Trade Secrets resulted in a 55-month head start benefit for Akoustis.

findings.proposition: In its statement of intended proof, Qorvo states that an injunction is warranted to stop Akoustis promoting polycrystalline products as "single crystal", and that it is owed $1,146,604 in corrective-advertising damages on its false-advertising claim.
findings.target: Qorvo v. Akoustis, D. Del. 1:21-cv-01417: Qorvo's requested Lanham Act false-advertising relief
findings.speaker: Qorvo

spans.quote: An injunction is warranted to enjoin Akoustis from falsely promoting polycrystalline products as “single crystal.” 42. Qorvo is also owed damages of $1,146,604 for corrective advertising that addresses Akoustis’s false claims.

findings.proposition: In its statement of intended proof on the North Carolina Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act claim, Qorvo states it is owed $809,772 for the cost to recruit, hire and train replacement employees, and $66.1 million representing Akoustis's unjust enrichment from the unfair and deceptive practices.
findings.target: Qorvo v. Akoustis, D. Del. 1:21-cv-01417: Qorvo's requested UDTPA damages
findings.speaker: Qorvo

spans.quote: Qorvo is owed damages of $809,772 for the cost to recruit, hire, and train additional employees.
Qorvo is owed $66.1 million, representing the amount by which Akoustis has been unjustly enriched by its unfair and deceptive trade practices.

The unfair and deceptive acts also caused Qorvo actual injury, including the loss of its confidential information and the cost to Qorvo to recruit and re-train employees to take the place of the employees that Akoustis recruited for improper purposes.

findings.proposition: In its statement of intended proof on civil conspiracy, Qorvo states it is owed damages of $66.1 million for Akoustis's conspiracy to misappropriate its trade secrets and is also entitled to punitive damages; it names Akoustis's CEO Jeff Shealy and other officers as conspiracy members.

Members of this civil conspiracy include, but are not limited to, Jeff Shealy (Akoustis’s CEO)

findings.proposition: Qorvo's statement of intended proof says it will not pursue Count IV (false patent marking) or Count VII (RICO) at trial, and that in addition to compensatory, punitive, treble, exemplary, royalty and unjust-enrichment damages it seeks permanent injunctive relief, costs, pre- and post-judgment interest, attorneys' fees and disgorgement.

findings.proposition: At the close of Qorvo's case, Akoustis made two oral Rule 50(a) motions; the court (Judge McCalla) denied the first, which challenged Qorvo's trade-secret damages experts under Daubert/Rule 702, and reserved ruling on the second, which argued insufficient evidence of actual injury under the North Carolina UDTPA.
findings.target: Qorvo v. Akoustis, D. Del. 1:21-cv-01417: Akoustis's Rule 50(a) motions at trial

spans.quote: At the close of Pla intiff’s case, Defendants ’ made two oral Motions pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 50(a). The Court denied the first motion, which related to a Daubert/Fed. R. Civ. P. 702 challenge to Plaintiffs ’ Trade Secret Damages Experts, but reserved ruling on the second.
Defendants’ 50(a) motion argued that there is insufficient evidence to support a finding of actual injury to Plaintiff under the North Carolina Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act.

findings.proposition: On 14 May 2024 (D.I. 590) the court granted in part and denied in part Akoustis's second Rule 50(a) motion: there is sufficient evidence of actual injury for UDTPA liability, but the jury has no reasonable basis to find compensable damages under the UDTPA, because Qorvo's only damages basis (head-start benefit to Akoustis under the DTSA) is not cognizable under the UDTPA.
findings.target: Qorvo v. Akoustis, D. Del. 1:21-cv-01417: court ruling on UDTPA damages (D.I. 590)

spans.quote: Because Plaintiff’s only basis for proving damages to a reasonable certainty is inconsistent with the damages cognizable under the UDTPA, the Defendants’ 50(a) Motion is GRANTED IN PART AND DENIED IN PART. The jury has no reasonable basis to find compensable damages under the UDTPA, but has sufficient basis to find injury.
IT IS SO ORDERED, this 14th day of May, 2024.
Plaintiffs base their damages assessment exclusively on the DT SA’s head start benefit damages provision.

findings.proposition: In D.I. 590 the court found that Qorvo has not provided any evidence that it lost market share or suffered lost profit because of the alleged misappropriation, and no evidence that the parties compete in the same geographic area for the same customers; head-start benefits are not a proxy for damage to Qorvo.
findings.target: Qorvo v. Akoustis, D. Del. 1:21-cv-01417: record on Qorvo's actual loss (court's assessment, D.I. 590)

spans.quote: Plaintiff has not provided any evidence that they lost market share or suffered lost profit because of Defendants’ alleged misappropriation. Indeed, while there is testimony that the Parties are competitors, there is no evidence in the record that they compete in the same geographic area, for the same customers at each others’ expense.
As such, head start benefits are not a proxy for the damage to Plaintiff
But there is no evidence in the record that those revenues otherwise would have gone t o Plaintiffs, or that they resulted in any expansion of market share at Plaintiffs’ expense.

findings.proposition: In its motion to exclude (D.I. 476), Akoustis argues that Bennis's head-start theory compares the time value of revenue Akoustis actually received with revenue delayed by 55 months, that revenue is not a cognizable basis for unjust enrichment except in calculating ill-gotten profits, which Bennis does not calculate because Akoustis has never earned a profit, and that she includes all of Akoustis's historical revenue, including revenue unrelated to any alleged trade-secret use.
findings.target: Qorvo v. Akoustis, D. Del. 1:21-cv-01417: Akoustis's challenge to Qorvo's head-start damages method and revenue base
findings.speaker: Akoustis

spans.quote: it is based on a comparison of the “time value” of bare revenue that Akoustis actually received versus the revenue it allegedly would have received if that revenue had been delayed by 55 months. Revenue, however, is not a cognizable basis for calculating unjust enrichment except as part of the calculation of a defendant’s “ill-gotten” profits – something that Ms. Bennis does not purport to calculate, as Akoustis has never earned a profit.
even if revenue were a proper basis for unjust enric hment damages (it is not), Ms. Bennis errs by including in her revenue
calculation all of Akoustis’ historical revenue, including revenue unrelated to any alleged use of Qorvo’s purported trade secrets.

findings.speaker: Akoustis

spans.quote: As of March 31, 2024, the Company had cash and cash equivalents of $ 15.2 million and working capital of $ 10.3 million. findings.proposition: Akoustis's 10-Q (Note 2) states that an adverse judgment in the Delaware Trial (Qorvo v. Akoustis, D. Del. 1:21-cv-01417) would reduce how long it could operate on current cash and create an urgent need for additional liquidity or result in it curtailing or ceasing operations and filing a voluntary bankruptcy petition, and that these matters raise substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern within one year.
findings.target: Akoustis Technologies, Inc.: going-concern doubt and bankruptcy statement tied to the Qorvo trial
findings.speaker: Akoustis

spans.quote: Furthermore, an adverse judgment against the Company in the trial with respect to Qorvo Inc. vs. Akoustis Technologies, Inc. DE Case 1:21-cv-01417-JPM , as described below under Note 14. Commitments and Contingencies (the “Delaware Trial”), would reduce the amount of time that the Company could continue operating with its current cash resources, and create an urgent need for additional liquidity or result in the Company’s curtailing or ceasing operations and seeking protection by filing a voluntary petition for relief under the Bankruptcy Code. findings.proposition: In D.I. 553 the court held that Akoustis's argument that Bennis errs by including all of Akoustis's historical revenue in her calculation raises a question for the jury, not a basis for exclusion; Bennis's inclusion of all revenue rests on the opinion that the alleged trade secrets related to virtually every aspect of Akoustis's business (including grant money, fabrication, engineering services and manufacturing) and that its products reached market 55 months earlier.
findings.target: Qorvo v. Akoustis, D. Del. 1:21-cv-01417: revenue base in Qorvo's head-start damages left to the jury (D.I. 553)

spans.quote: Defendants’ argument that Ms. Bennis errs by including in her revenue calculation all of Akoustis’ historical revenue raises a question for the jury, not a basis for exclusion under Rule 702.

In forming her opinion that all revenue should be included in the damages calculation, Ms. Bennis incorporates the opinion of Dr. Shanfield in finding that “the trade secrets Akoustis [are] alleged to have misappropriated related to virtually every aspect of its business and ability to get to market in the timeframe it did [including] its ability to earn grant money, fabricate products, provide engineering services, and manufacture products[,]” and that the Akoustis products were brought to market 55 months earlier than they would have without the alleged trade secrets.

findings.proposition: In its reply (D.I. 508), Akoustis describes Bennis's head-start method as taking all of Akoustis's revenue from 2016 through 30 June 2024 regardless of source, shifting it 55 months into the future, and computing its time value at Akoustis's WACC as of 30 June 2024; Qorvo's opposition (D.I. 496) states Akoustis argues the method fails to exclude revenue from federal grants, the MEMS facility, RFMi and the GDSI acquisition, which Qorvo calls fodder for cross-examination.

spans.quote: Using all of Akoustis’ revenue regardless of source or character, she calculated its “time value” based on Akoustis’ WACC as of June 30, 2024. She then shifted all of Akoustis’ revenue from 2016 through June 30, 2024 – 55 months in the future – and used the WACC to calculate its time value as of June 30, 2024.

Th ese complaints are classic ex amples of “fodder for cross.”

findings.proposition: D.I. 590 states that North Carolina courts have upheld UDTPA liability even where juries awarded only nominal damages; that UDTPA damage categories are narrower than the DTSA's; that North Carolina allows disgorgement of a defendant's profits as damages where they proxy for the plaintiff's injury but has not recognized head-start benefits as such a proxy; and that lost profits and lost market share from accelerated market entry are permissible UDTPA damage bases when sales were in the same area and products.
findings.target: Qorvo v. Akoustis, D. Del. 1:21-cv-01417: UDTPA damages law as stated in D.I. 590

spans.quote: Carolina courts have upheld liability findings even where juries have awarded only nominal damages.
The categories of damages cognizable under the UDTPA, however, are more limited than those cognizable under the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act.

North Carolina Courts have allowed for disgorgement of profits by defendants to serve as damages where they are proxies for injury by plaintiff, but has not recognized head start benefits to the Defendants as such a proxy.
Plaintiffs are not required to s how exact dollar amounts with mathe matical precision, but must prove damages to a reasonable certaint y.

Lost profits and “lost market share resulting from defendants’ accelerated market entry” have been held to be permissible bases for damages under the UDTPA when sales were made in the same geographic area and of the same products.
